## Wooden Rails and Horse Power

The railway did not appear as a single invention. It grew out of a long practice of moving heavy loads along prepared surfaces, and the earliest form of that practice was the simplest. Where a road was muddy, uneven, or steep, people laid planks, stones, or timber sleepers beneath the wheels of a cart so that the wheels ran more smoothly and the animal pulling the load could move more weight. Some of the oldest surviving examples are associated with the Greek world. The Diolkos, a paved trackway across the Isthmus of Corinth, carried ships on wheeled wooden cradles from one gulf to the other. It was in use by about the sixth century BC, and it is often cited as an early ancestor of the railway because its paving guided the wheels and reduced friction. Its purpose was transport over a barrier, not the speed of a journey, but the principle of a guided wheel was already present.

The more direct ancestors of the railway were built in the mining districts of central Europe and England during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Mines needed to move ore, waste rock, and water out of pits, and the distances underground and on the surface were often short but the loads were heavy. Wooden rails, sometimes capped with iron strips, allowed small wagons to run on flanged or unflanged wheels with less resistance than carts on rough ground. Georgius Agricola, whose treatise on mining and metallurgy appeared in 1556, described and illustrated the practice of moving ore carts along timber guides in German mines. Mine wagonways of this kind were widespread in the Harz and Erzgebirge regions, and similar arrangements existed in Shropshire, Derbyshire, and the north of England.

In Britain the wagonway developed into a larger and more formal institution in the coal-producing districts of the northeast. Coal was heavy, bulky, and of low value per ton, which meant that the cost of moving it overland to a river or a coast could easily exceed the cost of the coal itself at the pithead. Coal owners therefore built wagonways from their collieries down to the banks of the Tyne and Wear, where the coal could be loaded into keel boats or ships. Early wagonways of this sort are recorded from the end of the sixteenth century, and by the eighteenth they formed a dense network around Newcastle and Sunderland. Horses pulled the wagons, which were usually hauled in trains of several vehicles, with the horse walking beside or behind the leading wagon and a boy or man controlling the brakes. The Causey Arch, a single-span stone bridge built in 1725 and 1726 for a wagonway in County Durham, shows how seriously these lines were engineered. It is one of the earliest large railway structures in the world, and it still stands.

The wagonways of this period were not railways in the modern sense, but they established several of the principles that later railways would depend on. The wheel was guided by the track, so the vehicle did not need to be steered. The surface was prepared to be smooth and level within limits, so that friction and rolling resistance were low. Trains were formed by coupling vehicles together, so that a single animal or engine could move a large mass. And the economics of the enterprise depended on volume: a wagonway was worth building only if it carried enough traffic over many years to repay the cost of the land, the rails, and the labour. The wagonway was thus an enterprise of the mine owner or the industrialist rather than of the carrier or the public, and this would shape the railway for much of its early history.

## Iron Rails and the Problem of Wear

Wood was the normal rail material for centuries, but it had obvious limitations. A timber rail wore quickly under the iron wheels of heavy wagons, and it rotted, split, and needed frequent replacement. Iron offered a better surface. In the eighteenth century, as iron production expanded in Shropshire, South Wales, and the north of England, ironmasters began experimenting with rails made of cast iron. The earliest cast-iron rails were L-shaped or fish-belly in section, and they were laid on stone blocks or timber sleepers. Abraham Darby III's Coalbrookdale works supplied cast-iron plateways in the 1760s and 1770s, and the Hay tramroad in Wales and the Lake Lock tramway in Shropshire are examples of lines of this period.

There were two main forms of iron track. A plateway had flat rails on which the wheels ran, and the flanged wheels of the wagons were guided by a flange on the wheel rather than by a rail edge. A edgeway, sometimes called the edge rail, had a raised rail on which a flangeless wheel ran, with the rail edge providing the guidance. Edge rails proved more durable and easier to keep clean, and over time they came to dominate. The brittleness of cast iron meant that rails broke under heavy loads, however, and the switch to wrought iron, which could be rolled into longer and tougher sections, came gradually in the early nineteenth century. Joseph Hewes's patent for a wrought-iron rail appeared in the 1790s, and by the 1810s wrought iron was being used in some of the most demanding lines.

The problem of weight was not confined to the rail. The wagons themselves, with their wooden bodies and iron tyres, were heavy relative to their load, and the horses that drew them were limited in what they could pull on a continuous gradient. Iron rails reduced the rolling resistance of the wagon, but on a line with a long incline a horse could only do so much. Engineers responded with inclined planes, on which loaded wagons descended under gravity while empty ones were hauled back up, often by a rope passing over a drum at the top of the incline and driven by a stationary engine. Inclined planes were used in many of the early lines of Britain and the United States, and they remained part of railway engineering for a surprisingly long time. The Cromford and High Peak Railway, opened in 1831 and built to a design by Josias Jessop, had a series of inclined planes worked by water power and stationary steam engines, and it is a valuable record of how an engineer of the period might solve the problem of a steep gradient without a locomotive.

Iron rails and inclined planes were thus the immediate context in which the steam locomotive appeared. The wagonway had reached a point at which the track was good enough to carry a much heavier load than before, and the limitation was no longer the rail but the motive power. Horses were expensive to feed and house, they tired after a few hours, and they could not work continuously. The engine that could replace them was already in existence in a form that had been developed for other purposes, but it was far too heavy and too bulky to be placed on wheels. The railway's central problem for the next half-century was the making of an engine light enough to run on the track and strong enough to pull the loads that justified it.

## The Steam Engine Before the Locomotive

The stationary steam engine had a history of its own long before it was connected to a railway. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine, first built in 1712 near Dudley, used steam to raise a piston in a cylinder, which was then condensed by a spray of cold water so that the atmospheric pressure pushed the piston down. It was a slow, heavy, and fuel-hungry machine, but it could pump water from mines, and it was adopted widely in the coalfields where coal was cheap and the pumping problem severe. Newcomen engines were built in large numbers across Britain, Germany, and elsewhere, and they were the principal means of keeping deep mines dry in the first half of the eighteenth century.

James Watt's improvements, begun in the 1760s and patented in 1769, transformed the steam engine. Watt added a separate condenser, so that the cylinder was kept hot and the steam was condensed in a different vessel. This saved a great deal of fuel. Later he developed a double-acting engine in which steam pushed the piston in both directions, and he devised a mechanism for converting reciprocating motion into rotary motion, which allowed steam power to drive machinery in mills and factories. Watt's engines were manufactured with his partner Matthew Boulton at the Soho Foundry in Birmingham, and they were supplied across Britain and beyond. The engine became a general-purpose source of power, and its diffusion through the textile, metalworking, and mining industries gave a powerful impetus to the idea that steam could move things other than water.

Watt himself was cautious about high-pressure steam, and he believed that high-pressure engines were dangerous. Richard Trevithick, a Cornish engineer, disagreed. Trevithick's engines used steam at much higher pressures than Watt's, and because they did not need a separate condenser they could be made smaller and lighter. In 1801 Trevithick built a steam carriage, the Puffing Devil, which carried passengers on a road at Camborne in Cornwall. It was not a success, and the road was too rough, but it demonstrated that a steam engine could be mounted on wheels. Trevithick then turned his attention to the problem of running an engine on a plateway. In 1804 he built a locomotive at the Penydarren ironworks near Merthyr Tydfil in South Wales, and on 21 February of that year it hauled a train of wagons carrying about ten tons of iron and around seventy men along a tramroad of roughly nine miles.

The Penydarren engine was a remarkable achievement and a failure at the same time. It was the first recorded run of a steam locomotive on rails, and it proved that the idea was technically feasible. But the cast-iron plates of the tramroad were not strong enough to bear the engine's weight without breaking, and the engine was too heavy for the track. Trevithick did not pursue the locomotive, and he moved on to other projects, including a steam dredger and a steam-powered threshing machine. The locomotive was thus the product of a particular set of conditions: a high-pressure engine, a plateway capable of bearing a moderate load, and an ironworks that needed to move iron from furnace to canal. Trevithick's successors would have to solve the problem of weight and traction more thoroughly.

Trevithick's engine was also shaped by a theoretical question that occupied engineers for years: whether a smooth iron wheel running on a smooth iron rail could grip sufficiently to pull a train. Some engineers believed that friction would be inadequate and that the wheels would spin. Others argued that the adhesion of a smooth wheel on a smooth rail was sufficient for moderate loads. The question was answered by practice rather than by theory, and by the time the Liverpool and Manchester Railway was being planned in the 1820s it was generally accepted that adhesion was enough. Nevertheless, several designers tried to avoid the problem altogether, most notably by building rack locomotives that engaged a toothed rail.

## Blenkinsop, Hedley, and the Stephensons

The first commercially useful steam locomotives were built in the northeast of England, in the same coalfields where the horse-drawn wagonways had flourished. John Blenkinsop, the manager of the Middleton Colliery near Leeds, was troubled by the difficulty of getting a locomotive to grip a smooth rail, and in 1811 he took out a patent for a locomotive that worked on a rack. The rail had cogs cast on one side, and the engine's driving wheel had teeth that engaged them. The Salamanca, built by Matthew Murray's works in Holbeck and running on the Middleton Railway from 1812, is generally regarded as the first commercially successful steam locomotive. It hauled coal wagons for several years, and it is an example of how practical needs could produce a machine that was ingenious but inelegant.

The rack was not the only solution. William Hedley, working at Wylam Colliery near Newcastle, built a locomotive in 1813 that ran on a smooth rail and used a multiple-cylinder arrangement and a light frame to achieve enough adhesion. The machine, later known as Puffing Billy, is preserved in the Science Museum in London and is one of the oldest surviving locomotives in the world. Hedley's engine ran for many years on the Wylam wagonway, and it showed that a smooth rail and an adequately designed engine could work well enough for the coal trade. Puffing Billy was an early example of a locomotive that did a practical job for a long time, and its survival makes it one of the most important objects in the history of the railway.

George Stephenson, a self-taught engineer who had worked as a brakesman and then as an engine fireman at Killingworth colliery, built his first locomotive in 1814. The engine, called Blücher, ran on the Killingworth wagonway and hauled coal wagons. Stephenson was a shrewd and practical engineer, and he understood the economics of the coal trade better than most of his contemporaries. He improved the design of locomotives step by step, adding more efficient boilers, better valve gear, and strong frames, and in doing so he established a model that other builders copied. His son Robert, trained in the workshops at Newcastle, became one of the most important locomotive engineers of his generation, and the firm that bore the family name supplied engines for many of the early lines.

Stephenson's most famous contribution was not, however, the locomotive but the safety lamp. In 1815 he devised a lamp for miners that was intended to protect against the explosive gas known as firedamp, working independently of Humphry Davy, whose lamp was announced at about the same time. The rivalry between the two lamps became a controversy in the scientific community, and Stephenson's reputation in the northeast was enhanced by his association with the rescue and protection of miners. The incident is a reminder that the early railway engineers were often men of the mine, and that their concerns were bound up with the safety and productivity of the collieries.

The conditions of the northeast coal trade favoured the development of the locomotive because the wagonways were already in place, the coal owners were rich enough to pay for experiments, and the traffic was heavy and regular. Steam locomotives were most useful where the wagons were already moving large quantities of goods over long distances, and where the cost of horses or stationary engines was high. The coal fields thus became a laboratory for locomotive design, and the engines built there were copied and improved across the country. By the early 1820s Stephenson and his contemporaries had established that a steam locomotive could work reliably, though they had not yet demonstrated that it could carry passengers or travel at high speed.

## The Stockton and Darlington Line

The Stockton and Darlington Railway, promoted by Quaker merchants and coal interests in County Durham, was authorised by Parliament in 1821 and opened on 27 September 1825. It was the first public railway in the sense that it was open to any carrier who paid the toll, rather than a private line serving a single colliery or ironworks. Its promoters had originally intended to use horse power, and most of the traffic on the line in its early years was indeed horse-drawn. But the line's engineer, George Stephenson, was persuaded to build a steam locomotive for the opening, and the engine, Locomotion No. 1, was built at the Forth Street works in Newcastle. It hauled a train of coal wagons and several passenger carriages on the opening day, and it is generally recognised as the first steam locomotive to haul a public passenger train.

The Stockton and Darlington was not a conspicuous success as a steam railway. Stephenson's locomotives were slow and unreliable compared with the horses that continued to do most of the work, and the company used steam locomotives only for part of its traffic. The line also had a mixed set of gradients and curves, and it was built to a relatively light standard. Nevertheless, the line demonstrated that a public railway could be built and operated, and that steam traction could be used on it. The company's example encouraged other promoters to consider railways as a means of general transport, and it made clear that the wagonway could be turned into a common carrier open to all traffic.

Passengers on the Stockton and Darlington were carried in coaches that were built on the model of stagecoach bodies, and the early passenger service was often drawn by horses. The company introduced a timetable and fares, and it gradually expanded its passenger traffic through the 1830s. Its trains were not fast, but they were regular, and they showed that people would travel by rail if the service was dependable. The line also influenced the political debate in Parliament, where the question of whether railways should be treated as public highways or private property was contested. The Stockton and Darlington was a common carrier, and this principle was carried forward in the legislation of the 1830s and 1840s.

The line's construction also revealed the costs of building a railway in a settled country. The land had to be bought from many owners, the Act of Parliament had to be passed, and the engineering works had to be carried out in ways that avoided damaging the property of neighbours. These costs and procedures became standard features of railway promotion, and they made railways very different from the wagonways that had preceded them. A railway was a public undertaking, subject to the legislative process and to the scrutiny of landowners, and it required capital from investors who expected a return.

## The Rainhill Trials and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway

The true starting point of the modern railway is generally held to be the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, which was authorised by Parliament in 1826 after a bitter contest with canal and turnpike interests. The line was intended to link the port of Liverpool with the textile city of Manchester, a distance of about thirty miles, and its promoters believed that a railway could carry both goods and passengers faster and more cheaply than the existing canal. The company's engineers, notably George Stephenson and his colleague John Dixon, designed a route with relatively few steep gradients, but the crossing of Chat Moss, a boggy peat bog, presented enormous difficulties. The line was built with embankments and a great deal of ingenuity, and it was an important demonstration of what railway engineers could achieve with earth and rock.

The directors of the company were not sure whether to use stationary engines, horses, or locomotives. To resolve the question, they held a competition at Rainhill, near Liverpool, in October 1829. The competition, known as the Rainhill Trials, offered a prize of five hundred pounds for the locomotive that best met a set of demanding conditions. The engine had to weigh no more than six tons, pull a load of several times its own weight at a specified speed, and run a set distance over the course without breakdown. The contest attracted several entrants, but the field was dominated by the Stephensons' engine, the Rocket, built with the assistance of Henry Booth, the company's treasurer, who had suggested the multitubular boiler. The Rocket used a large number of small tubes to conduct the hot gases through the boiler, which greatly increased the heating surface and the efficiency of steam production.

The Rocket won the trials, reaching a speed that was remarkable for the period, and it set the pattern for the locomotives that would follow. Its layout, with a sloping cylinder driving the wheels through connecting rods, a multitubular boiler, and a blast pipe that drew the fire through the tubes, became the basis of the classic locomotive. The Rainhill trials were therefore both a contest and a turning point, establishing the viability of the steam locomotive for passenger traffic at speeds that had been thought impossible only a few years earlier.

The line opened on 15 September 1830 with a great ceremony. The Duke of Wellington, then Prime Minister, attended the opening, and the train carrying the dignitaries was hauled by the locomotive Northumbrian. During a stop at Parkside, the MP William Huskisson, who had been a senior government minister and a supporter of the railway, stepped onto the track to speak with the Duke and was struck by the Rocket, which had been brought to the scene on a second train. Huskisson was badly injured and died later that evening. His death was the first fatality of a passenger on a steam railway in the world, and it was a shocking event that received wide attention. It also highlighted the new dangers of railway travel and the need for rules about the separation of trains from pedestrians and from the public.

The Liverpool and Manchester was a commercial success. It carried large numbers of passengers and goods, and its traffic grew quickly. The company paid dividends, the line was widely imitated, and the engineers who had built it became the leading figures of the railway profession. The line also established several practices that would become standard: a double track with signalled sections, timetables, a set of rules for trains, and the use of locomotives for both passengers and goods. For many people it was the moment when the railway ceased to be a curiosity and became a serious means of transport.

## The Spread of Railways in Britain

The success of the Liverpool and Manchester encouraged a wave of railway projects across Britain in the 1830s and 1840s. Many were promoted by merchants and manufacturers who saw the railway as a way of connecting markets, and some were promoted by investors who were attracted by the prospect of dividends. The London and Birmingham Railway, the first main line to connect the capital with the Midlands, was completed in 1838 after a long construction period, and it was followed by lines radiating from London and from the major provincial cities. The Great Western Railway, promoted by Isambard Kingdom Brunel, was opened between London and Bristol in 1841, and it was notable for its broad gauge of seven feet and a quarter inch, which Brunel believed would provide greater stability and speed than the standard gauge then used by most lines.

The standard gauge of four feet eight and a half inches had a long pedigree, and it was used by the Stockton and Darlington, the Liverpool and Manchester, and the London and Birmingham. The gauge was derived from the spacing of the wheels of the wagons used in the northeast coal trade, and it had been inherited by the early railway engineers. The coexistence of broad and standard gauges created a practical problem, because trains could not run from one system to the other and goods had to be transhipped at the boundaries. Parliament eventually addressed the problem in the Gauge Act of 1846, which required new lines to be built to the standard gauge except where the broad gauge was already established, and a royal commission had reported on the question in 1845 in favour of standardisation. The broad gauge survived in the west of England until 1892, when the last of it was converted, and its disappearance was a striking example of the advantages of uniform standards in a network.

The 1840s also saw the most famous episode in the history of British railway investment, the period known as Railway Mania. Between 1844 and 1847 the number of railway companies seeking parliamentary approval rose enormously, and the sums of capital proposed ran into the hundreds of millions of pounds. Many of the schemes were speculative, and many of them were never built. Investors, attracted by the prospect of high dividends and rapid appreciation of shares, bought stock in companies that existed only on paper. The collapse of the market in 1847 ruined many investors and left a great many unfinished or unprofitable lines. Yet the mania also produced a dense network of railways in a short time, and it established the rail system that would carry Britain through the rest of the nineteenth century. Some of the lines built during the mania became the backbone of the national network, and the speculative boom was thus, in its way, a substantial contribution to the physical infrastructure of the country.

The government responded to the excesses of the mania with legislation that set the terms of railway operation for decades. The Railway Regulation Act of 1844, often called the Gladstone Act after William Gladstone, who was then President of the Board of Trade, required companies to run a daily train for third-class passengers at a speed of at least twelve miles an hour and at a fare of one penny per mile. It also gave the state the right to purchase lines after twenty-one years, though this right was rarely exercised. The act established the principle that railways were a public service with obligations to the public, and it began a long tradition of regulation that would expand over the following century.

Railway timetables and time itself were transformed by the spread of the network. Before the railways, most towns kept local time based on the position of the sun, and the difference between towns could be several minutes. When railways began to run trains on schedules across long distances, this variation became a serious problem, and the Great Western Railway adopted Greenwich Mean Time for its timetables in 1840, followed by other companies. Greenwich time became the standard for the railway network and eventually for the country as a whole, and a national standard was formally established by the Statutes (Definition of Time) Act of 1880. The railway's need for accurate and uniform time was thus one of the drivers of the modern concept of standard time. The timetable itself, published in the form of the Bradshaw guide from 1839, became a central part of the travelling public's experience of the railway.

## Excursions, Tourism, and the Social Reach of the Railway

The railway was not only a freight system and a means of commuting; it also changed how people spent their leisure. The earliest railway excursions were organised for religious, political, or charitable purposes, but the most famous early example of commercial excursion travel is generally held to be the trip organised by Thomas Cook in 1841, when he chartered a train to carry temperance supporters from Leicester to a meeting at Loughborough. Cook went on to organise a large business of tourist travel, and by the 1860s his firm was arranging continental tours and then world tours. The railway made it possible for people of modest means to travel distances that had previously been reserved for the wealthy, and it created a new kind of mass tourism based on regular, scheduled, and affordable journeys.

Seaside resorts were among the greatest beneficiaries of the railway. Places such as Brighton, Blackpool, Scarborough, and Margate grew rapidly in the nineteenth century as railways carried visitors from industrial cities to the coast for a day or a week. The railway gave working people a means of escaping the city and of experiencing the sea, and it helped to create the holiday as a regular feature of urban life. Similar developments took place in continental Europe, where railways carried visitors to spas, mountains, and cities of cultural importance, and in the United States, where the growth of railway travel created resorts in the mountains and along the coasts.

The railway also changed the geography of settlement. Commuting became possible for people who worked in cities but lived in suburbs, and the railway suburb became a characteristic feature of the expanding metropolis. Londoners could live in Croydon or Surbiton and travel to work in the city; Parisians could live in the rapidly growing communes around the capital; New Yorkers and Chicagoans could move to suburbs served by commuter lines. In many cities the railway station became a centre of commercial and social life, with hotels, restaurants, and shops clustered around the terminal. The station itself was a monument to the confidence of the nineteenth century, often built on a grand scale and decorated with iron and glass.

Railways also made possible a new kind of news. Newspapers could be printed in the morning and carried by rail to distant readers within hours, and the railway mail service allowed letters and parcels to move faster than ever before. The telegraph, which spread alongside the railway, was frequently laid along the track, and the two technologies became partners in the rapid transmission of information and goods. The combined effect was to create a sense of a national and then international community bound together by fast connections, and this sense became a powerful feature of modern life.

## The Railway in the United States

Railways developed in the United States with a different character from those in Britain. The American landscape was vast and sparsely populated in many regions, the capital was scarce, and the public was suspicious of large corporations. Early American lines were built by private companies, often with the support of state governments, and the typical railway was short and local. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, chartered in 1827, is generally regarded as the first major American railway, and it was built with the aim of linking the port of Baltimore with the Ohio River and the markets of the interior. The company was in competition with the Erie Canal and with the canal projects of Pennsylvania and Virginia, and it had to struggle against both canal interests and political opposition.

The Baltimore and Ohio adopted a range of locomotive designs in its early years. Peter Cooper built a small experimental locomotive, Tom Thumb, in 1830 to demonstrate the feasibility of steam traction on the company's line, and the engine is remembered for a race with a horse-drawn car, which Tom Thumb is said to have been winning until its belt slipped. The story is often told as an illustration of the superiority of horses over steam at that time, though it is also a reminder that early locomotives were unreliable and experimental. The company later imported British locomotives and built its own, and it was among the first American railways to use the commercial steam locomotive on a regular basis.

Several American engineers and manufacturers developed locomotive designs that suited the conditions of their country. American railways were often built with lighter track and tighter curves than British railways, and they had to cope with variable traffic and limited capital. The American locomotive developed its own distinctive features: the four-wheeled leading truck, which improved stability on curves; the cowcatcher, a wedge-shaped frame at the front of the locomotive designed to clear livestock from the track; and the wood-burning stack, which reflected the abundance of timber in many regions. The so-called American type, with a four-wheel leading truck and two driving axles, became one of the most common locomotive layouts in the world in the nineteenth century. Its adaptability made it popular across the expanding networks of the United States and beyond.

The growth of American railways was rapid and uneven. By the 1850s the network extended from the Atlantic coast into the Midwest, and by the 1860s it had reached the Mississippi and beyond. The railway was a central factor in the economic development of the country, carrying grain, cattle, timber, coal, and manufactured goods, and it helped to create the great cities of Chicago, Saint Louis, and Kansas City. Railway companies received land grants from the federal and state governments, and in some cases they were allowed to sell land along their routes to settlers. These grants gave the railways a stake in the settlement of the interior and encouraged the spread of farms and towns along the lines.

The transcontinental railroad was the most ambitious American railway project of the nineteenth century. The Pacific Railroad Acts of 1862 and 1864 authorised two companies, the Central Pacific and the Union Pacific, to build lines from California and from the Missouri River respectively, and the two lines were to meet in the middle of the continent. The Central Pacific workforce was drawn heavily from Chinese labourers, who did much of the dangerous work of blasting and tunnelling through the Sierra Nevada. The Union Pacific employed many Irish and European workers, along with former soldiers. The two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah on 10 May 1869, when a golden spike was driven to mark the completion of the route. The transcontinental railroad drastically shortened the time needed to cross the continent, and it became a symbol of national unity and industrial progress. It also transformed the economies of the American West, bringing settlers, goods, and capital into regions that had previously been difficult to reach.

American railways developed a set of technologies and practices that were widely copied abroad. The Westinghouse air brake, patented in 1869, allowed a train's brakes to be applied simultaneously throughout the length of the train, greatly improving safety. George Westinghouse's invention became the standard braking system for American freight and passenger trains, and it was eventually adopted in many other countries. Automatic couplers, developed in the 1870s, replaced the dangerous practice of coupling by hand between cars, which had caused many injuries and deaths among brakemen. The American railway also pioneered the use of large freight wagons, the boxcar and the hopper car, and it developed systems of freight classification and rate-setting that became a model for railway management. Many of these developments were the product of intense competition between companies and of the need to reduce costs in a country where labour was expensive and distances were great.

The American railway was also the site of significant labour and political conflict. The Pullman strike of 1894, in which workers protested against wage cuts and the company's control of its town, led to a national crisis and the intervention of federal troops. The growth of large railway corporations raised concerns about monopoly and the abuse of power, and the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created the first federal regulatory agency in the United States, the Interstate Commerce Commission, to oversee rates and practices. The American railway thus became a central subject of political debate, and the question of how to regulate private enterprise for public benefit remained a significant issue for the rest of the century.

## Railways on the Continent

Continental Europe began building railways a few years after Britain, and it developed its networks in ways that reflected its different political and economic conditions. The first German railway, the Ludwigsbahn between Nuremberg and Fürth, opened in 1835, and it used a locomotive named Adler built by a British firm. The line was short, but it was a demonstration that railways could be built on the continent and that German industrial and commercial interests could benefit from them. German states were politically fragmented, and the railway networks of the 1830s and 1840s were built by separate states and companies, often with different gauges and different operating practices. The unification of Germany in 1871 brought the railways under a more coherent administration, though the Prussian state railways played a particularly important role in the new Reich.

Belgium was the first continental country to build a national railway network with state support. The line between Brussels and Mechelen, opened in 1835, was the first long-distance railway on the continent, and the Belgian government took a strong role in planning and building the national network. Belgium's industrial base in coal and iron provided a strong demand for railway transport, and its relatively small size made it possible to create a dense network within a short time. The Belgian example influenced other countries, and the principle of state-led railway development became a common feature of continental policy.

France was slower to build its network, partly because of the difficulties of agreeing on a national plan and partly because of the influence of canal and road interests. The first French railway, between Saint-Étienne and Lyon, opened in stages in the early 1830s, and it was built to serve the coal and textile industries of the region. The French government eventually adopted a plan of national lines radiating from Paris, and the Railway Act of 1842 provided for the construction of the main lines by private companies under state supervision. The result was a network dominated by six great companies, each with its own territory and its own locomotive and rolling-stock practices. The French system thus combined private enterprise with a strong degree of government direction, and it remained in this form until the nationalisation of the 1930s.

Russia built its first major railway, between Saint Petersburg and Tsarskoye Selo, in 1837, and the line was used to carry the imperial family and their guests as well as general traffic. The Moscow to Saint Petersburg line, begun in the 1840s and completed in 1851, was one of the most ambitious engineering projects in Europe at the time, and it was built to a broad gauge of five feet, which was adopted for Russian lines in order to make them difficult to invade by standard-gauge trains from the west. The Russian railway network expanded rapidly in the late nineteenth century, especially under the influence of the Trans-Siberian Railway, which was begun in 1891 and completed in stages until 1916. The Trans-Siberian was one of the longest railways in the world and a symbol of the expansion of the Russian state into Asia.

The Austro-Hungarian Empire developed its railways in a complex political environment, with lines built by private companies and by the state. The Kaiser Ferdinands-Nordbahn, which opened in 1837 between Vienna and Floridsdorf, was one of the earliest railways on the continent, and it was followed by lines to the north, south, and east. The empire's railways were important for the movement of troops and goods, and they played a role in the integration of the diverse territories of the monarchy. The Semmering route, opened in 1854, was an important engineering achievement, with a series of tunnels, viaducts, and steep gradients, and it showed that railways could be built across mountainous terrain.

Italy was divided into several states until the unification of the 1860s, and its railways were correspondingly fragmented. The first Italian railway, between Naples and Portici, opened in 1839, and it was built by the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Other lines followed in the Kingdom of Sardinia and in the states of central Italy, and the unification of the country gave impetus to a national network. The Mont Cenis tunnel, begun in the 1850s and completed in 1871, was a major achievement that connected Italy and France through the Alps, and it was among the longest railway tunnels in the world at the time.

Across Europe the railway became a central instrument of state power and national integration. Governments built railways to move troops, to link capitals with provinces, and to bind together territories that might otherwise have drifted apart. The railway was also a symbol of modernity, and political leaders used it to demonstrate their commitment to progress. The continental pattern was therefore shaped by the interplay of state strategy, private capital, and engineering ambition, and it produced networks that were both integrated and fragmented, depending on the politics of the country concerned.

## Locomotive Engineering in the Nineteenth Century

The locomotive went through a long process of development in the nineteenth century, and its engineers faced constant trade-offs between power, speed, weight, and reliability. The early locomotives of the 1820s and 1830s were small, light, and fast by the standards of the time, but they were limited in the loads they could pull and the gradients they could climb. As railways became longer and traffic heavier, engineers sought to build engines that could pull more and go faster, and they did so by increasing the size of boilers, adding wheels, and improving the efficiency of steam production.

The Stephensons' Patentee type, introduced in the 1830s, established the basic arrangement of two driving wheels and a leading pair of smaller wheels, and it was widely copied. The 2-2-2 layout was suitable for the light trains and modest speeds of the period, and it gave engines good riding characteristics on the track. As trains became heavier, engineers added more driving wheels and developed boilers with greater heating surfaces. The development of the 0-6-0 freight locomotive, with six coupled driving wheels and no leading truck, provided greater adhesion for heavy goods trains, and it became a common type on British and continental railways.

Express locomotives required larger driving wheels, to allow higher speeds without excessive piston speed, and engineers experimented with a variety of solutions. Thomas Russell Crampton designed a locomotive in the 1840s with a single large driving wheel and an outside cylinder arrangement, which was particularly popular on the continent, where the Crampton type was used on express trains in France, Belgium, and Germany. The Crampton's large wheel gave it high speed, but its single driving axle limited its adhesion and its ability to pull heavy loads, and it was eventually supplanted by more powerful designs.

The locomotive's valve gear was a particularly important area of development. The early locomotives used simple slide valves that were operated by eccentrics on the driving axle, and they were limited in their ability to vary the cut-off of steam and therefore in their efficiency. The Walschaerts valve gear, devised by the Belgian engineer Egide Walschaerts in 1844 and widely used in the twentieth century, provided a more flexible system for controlling steam admission and reversing the engine. The gear was adopted on many continental and later British locomotives, and its use allowed engines to run more efficiently at a range of speeds and loads. Other valve gear designs, including the Stephenson link motion, the Joy gear, and the Heusinger gear, were used in different countries and for different purposes, and the choice of valve gear was often a matter of national tradition as well as engineering merit.

Compounding was another important innovation. A compound locomotive used steam twice, first in a high-pressure cylinder and then in one or more low-pressure cylinders, which allowed the engine to extract more energy from the steam and to achieve greater efficiency. Compounding had been tried in the nineteenth century, but it became widespread in the early twentieth century, particularly in Europe, where it was used on a large number of express and heavy freight locomotives. The Mallet articulated locomotive, designed by the Swiss engineer Anatole Mallet and first used in the 1880s, combined two sets of driving wheels under a single boiler, allowing very heavy trains to be hauled on sharp curves and steep gradients. The Mallet was used extensively in mountain railways, in colonial railways, and in American logging and mining lines.

Superheating, the process of heating steam after it leaves the boiler, was one of the most significant technical advances of the early twentieth century. Superheated steam was drier and hotter, which reduced condensation in the cylinders and improved the efficiency of the engine. The Schmidt superheater, developed by Wilhelm Schmidt in the late nineteenth century and widely adopted from about 1900, became a standard feature of many European locomotives, and it allowed significant increases in power without enlarging the boiler. Superheating transformed the economics of steam traction and extended the working life of the steam locomotive well into the twentieth century.

The steam locomotive reached its peak of sophistication in the first half of the twentieth century. Designers built enormous engines for heavy freight and fast passenger service, including the Pacific and Mikado types in the United States, the Pacific and Mountain types in Europe, and the great express locomotives of Britain such as the Gresley Pacifics and the Stanier designs. These engines were symbols of national engineering prestige, and their design was the product of decades of accumulated experience. Yet they were also expensive to maintain, required large numbers of staff, and were inefficient compared with the diesel and electric traction that was beginning to challenge them. The steam locomotive was thus a triumph of engineering and an artefact of an older industrial economy.

## Safety, Signalling, and Communication

Railway safety was a continuing concern throughout the nineteenth century, and the development of signalling and communication systems was a crucial part of the railway's maturity. In the early years, trains were often run on the basis of simple rules and the judgment of individual drivers and guards, and collisions and derailments were common. As traffic increased and the network became more complex, the need for systematic control of train movements became more pressing. The development of the block system, which divided the line into sections and allowed only one train at a time within each section, was a major step forward. The system was based on signals and on the communication of train movements between signal boxes, and it became the standard method of controlling traffic on most railways.

The electric telegraph was an essential tool in this development. Cooke and Wheatstone's telegraph, first used on the Great Western Railway in the 1840s, allowed signalmen to communicate with one another about the position and movement of trains, and it made possible a level of coordination that would have been impossible with messengers or with visual signals alone. The telegraph was a powerful means of controlling traffic, and it was soon adopted across the railway networks of Britain, Europe, and North America. The combination of signals and telegraph gave railway managers a degree of control over their operations that had not previously existed.

The absolute block system, which prevented a second train from entering a section until the first had cleared it, was developed in Britain in the 1840s and 1850s and was made mandatory on the main lines of Britain by the 1889 Regulation of Railways Act, which followed a serious accident at Armagh in Northern Ireland in 1889. The Armagh disaster, in which a collision killed many passengers, was a catalyst for the strengthening of safety rules, and it underlined the importance of automatic and mechanical safeguards. The Regulation of Railways Act also required the installation of continuous automatic brakes on passenger trains, a requirement that accelerated the adoption of the vacuum brake in Britain and the Westinghouse air brake elsewhere.

The tablet and staff systems, devised to ensure that only one train occupied a single line of track at a time, were another important safety innovation. The train carried a physical token, such as a staff or a tablet, which allowed it to enter the section, and a second train could not enter without its own token. These mechanical devices were designed to prevent the most common cause of head-on collisions, which was the presence of two trains on the same line without proper authority. The tablet system was particularly important on single lines, where the risk of collision was especially high, and it remained in use in many countries well into the twentieth century.

Interlocking, in which signals and points were mechanically linked so that a signal could not be cleared unless the route was properly set, was another important development. Interlocked signalling reduced the chance of human error and made it possible to operate complex junctions and stations with fewer staff. Interlocking was introduced in the second half of the nineteenth century and became a standard feature of major stations and junctions. Later, electrical and electronic interlocking replaced mechanical systems in many places, and the signalling of modern railways is controlled by computer systems that combine the functions of interlocking, route setting, and train supervision.

Communication between train and control centre also developed over time. Early trains carried guards with flags, lamps, and whistles, and drivers relied on the signals along the line. The development of train radio in the twentieth century allowed drivers and controllers to communicate directly, and modern railways use digital radio systems to coordinate movements, report faults, and manage emergencies. The integration of these systems into automatic train protection, which can stop a train that passes a danger signal, has been one of the most significant safety advances of the late twentieth century.

## Electrification and the Electric Train

The idea of electric traction appeared early in the history of the railway, and electric railways were demonstrated in the 1830s and 1840s, though they were not practical at the time because batteries and generators were too heavy and too inefficient. The electric motor and the dynamo, developed in the later nineteenth century, made electric traction feasible, and the first practical electric railway was built by Werner von Siemens at the Berlin Trade Exhibition of 1879, where a small electric locomotive hauled a train of passenger carriages around a short circuit. The demonstration was a sensation, and it led to the construction of the Gross-Lichterfelde tramway in Berlin in 1881, which is often regarded as the first electric street railway in the world.

The first electric railway for passenger service in Britain was the Volk's Electric Railway, which opened in Brighton in 1883 and is still in operation in a shortened form. The railway used a third rail to supply current to the motors, and it carried passengers along the seafront. Electric traction was gradually adopted for urban and suburban services, where the frequent stopping and starting of trains made electric motors more efficient than steam locomotives. The City and South London Railway, opened in 1890, was the first deep-level electric underground railway in the world, and it demonstrated the potential of electric traction in dense urban environments. The London Underground, which grew from this beginning, became one of the largest electric railway systems in the world.

The growth of electric urban railways in the early twentieth century was rapid. Tramways and metros were built in many cities, and the electric multiple unit, in which each carriage had its own motor and the train could be controlled from the driving cab, became a standard feature of suburban services. The development of multiple-unit control systems, which allowed a train to be driven from any car, was a crucial advance, and it made possible the flexible operation of commuter networks. Sprague's multiple-unit system, developed in the United States in the 1890s, was an important early example, and similar systems were adopted in Britain, Germany, and elsewhere.

Electrification of main lines was more difficult and more expensive, because it required the construction of overhead wires or third rails along long distances and the design of locomotives capable of handling heavy trains. Several railways began electrifying their main lines in the early twentieth century. The Baltimore and Ohio electrified a tunnel in Baltimore in 1895, and the Pennsylvania Railroad electrified its approach to New York in the early 1900s. Italy and Switzerland pioneered the use of alternating current for main-line railways, and the Swiss Lötschberg line, electrified in 1913 with a single-phase system at low frequency, was an important early example. The choice between direct current and alternating current became one of the central questions of electric railway design, and different countries made different choices for technical and political reasons.

The electrification of railways in the mid-twentieth century was shaped by the rise of the electric power network and by the economics of coal and oil. Countries with large hydroelectric resources, such as Switzerland, Norway, and Sweden, electrified extensively, and the French network was progressively electrified after the Second World War. In the 1950s and 1960s the Netherlands, Germany, and Italy expanded their electrified networks, and the electrification of the trans-European routes became an important part of planning. Electric traction offered higher acceleration, lower operating costs, and cleaner operation in urban areas, and it became the preferred choice for intensively used main lines. The railway's shift to electric power changed the nature of the engineering profession, and it created a new generation of engineers skilled in power distribution, control systems, and electrical machinery.

## The Diesel Revolution

The internal combustion engine offered another route to railway modernisation, and diesel traction became a major force in the twentieth century. Diesel engines were efficient, could run for long periods without refuelling, and did not require the complex infrastructure of electrification. Early experiments with diesel locomotives were made in the 1910s and 1920s, but the diesel engine's power output was limited and its reliability poor. The development of the diesel-electric locomotive, in which a diesel engine drives a generator that supplies current to electric traction motors, solved many of these problems. The diesel-electric arrangement allowed the engine to run at its most efficient speed while the traction motors provided smooth and powerful drive across a range of speeds, and it made the diesel locomotive a practical and economical choice for many railways.

The diesel railcar, which carried passengers in a single unit with its own engine, was an earlier and more modest form of diesel traction. The Flying Hamburger, introduced by the German railway in 1933, was a streamlined diesel railcar that ran between Berlin and Hamburg at high speed for the time, and it became a symbol of the new era of railway design. The streamlined train, with its aerodynamic body and its lightweight construction, was part of a broader movement in the 1930s to modernise railway travel and to attract passengers from the road and the air. The Union Pacific's M-10000 streamliner and the Zephyr trains of the Burlington Railroad, introduced in the mid-1930s, were among the most famous examples of American streamlining, and they used diesel power to achieve high speeds over long distances.

The diesel-electric locomotive was widely adopted in the United States after the Second World War, and the General Motors Electro-Motive Division, which produced the famous F-units from the late 1930s onward, dominated the market. The F-unit, a streamlined diesel-electric locomotive with a powerful engine and a robust design, was used on passenger and freight trains across the continent, and it helped to make the diesel locomotive the standard form of traction in the United States. The shift from steam to diesel in the United States was remarkably rapid, and by the 1950s most American railways had retired their steam locomotives. The reasons for the change included the lower cost of diesel fuel, the reduced labour needs of diesel operation, and the greater reliability of the diesel locomotive.

In Britain the transition to diesel was slower and more controversial. The British Railways Modernisation Plan of 1955 proposed a massive programme of dieselisation and electrification, and it was a significant turning point in the country's railway history. The plan led to the construction of many diesel locomotives and multiple units, and it resulted in the withdrawal of steam locomotives over the following decade. The Deltic locomotive, a powerful diesel designed for the East Coast Main Line, was among the most celebrated British diesels, and it demonstrated the capacity of diesel traction for high-speed express service. The programme was not without difficulties, and some of its decisions were later criticised, but it transformed British railway operation.

Diesel traction also became important in other parts of the world. Railways in Africa, Asia, and South America adopted diesel locomotives for their long lines and their remote regions, where electrification was impractical. The diesel locomotive's independence from fixed infrastructure made it especially suitable for railways in developing economies, and it allowed countries to build and operate networks without the massive investment required for electrification. The diesel engine thus extended the reach of the railway into regions where the steam locomotive had been difficult to maintain and where electrification was too costly.

## The Speed Race and the Streamlined Era

The pursuit of speed has been one of the most visible features of railway history. Early locomotives were limited by the mechanical and thermal constraints of steam engines, and speeds of more than fifty or sixty miles an hour were rare until the later nineteenth century. In 1848 the Crampton locomotive Liverpool reached speeds of some sixty miles per hour on the London to Folkestone route, and in the 1890s the Dutch and French railways began to explore higher speeds with more powerful engines. The record for steam traction was set in 1938 by the British locomotive Mallard, an A4 class Pacific designed by Nigel Gresley for the London and North Eastern Railway. On 3 July 1938, Mallard reached a speed of 126 miles per hour (about 203 kilometres per hour) on a descent from Stoke Bank in Lincolnshire, and the record has never been surpassed by a steam locomotive.

The Mallard's record was achieved in a period of intense rivalry between railways and in the context of the streamlined design movement. Gresley's A4 class engines were fitted with streamlined casings, and the streamlined train, pioneered by the LNER with its Silver Jubilee service of 1935 and by the London Midland and Scottish Railway with its Coronation service of 1937, became a symbol of modernity and speed. The streamlining was partly aesthetic, reflecting the fashion of the 1930s, and partly functional, designed to reduce air resistance at high speeds. The Silver Jubilee and the Coronation were both designed to attract passengers from the road and to offer a luxurious and fast service between major cities.

The Second World War interrupted the development of high-speed railways in Europe and North America, and many lines were damaged by bombing. The postwar reconstruction of the railways was a major task, and the emphasis shifted to reliability, economy, and the modernisation of existing routes. The development of faster trains resumed in the 1950s and 1960s, with the introduction of new locomotives, electrified lines, and improved track. In France, the Électrotrain and the Turbotrain tested new forms of high-speed rail in the 1960s, and the Japanese National Railways began planning a new line that would make high-speed travel a practical reality.

The Tōkaidō Shinkansen, which opened between Tokyo and Osaka on 1 October 1964, was the first high-speed railway in the modern sense. It was built on a new standard-gauge line that was separated from the existing network, and it was designed for speeds of up to 210 kilometres per hour. The line was constructed under intense pressure to be ready for the Tokyo Olympics of 1964, and it was a remarkable achievement of engineering and organisation. The Shinkansen was soon carrying large numbers of passengers, and it demonstrated that a dedicated high-speed line could be profitable and safe. Its success led to the construction of further Shinkansen lines across Japan, and the network became a model for high-speed railways around the world.

The Shinkansen had a significant influence on railway design. Its separated right of way, its use of continuous welded rail, its signalling system, and its emphasis on punctuality and safety became standard features of later high-speed lines. The train's aerodynamic nose, its low-profile carriages, and its distributed traction system with powered axles in several cars were also copied in many subsequent designs. The Shinkansen's safety record has been notable, and no passenger has been killed in a derailment or collision on the system since it opened, although the network has been affected by earthquakes and other natural disasters. The line's punctuality, reliability, and ability to carry large numbers of passengers have made it an enduring example of what a high-speed railway can achieve.

## The French TGV and European High-Speed Rail

France took up the high-speed challenge in the late 1960s and 1970s, and the Train à Grande Vitesse, the TGV, became one of the most celebrated railway systems in the world. The French government decided in the 1970s to build a dedicated high-speed line between Paris and Lyon, and the line, known as LGV Sud-Est, opened in 1981 with services operating at up to 260 kilometres per hour. The line was designed with gentle curves and gradients, and it was equipped with new signalling and electrification systems. The TGV was a symbol of French technological prowess, and it helped to restore confidence in French industry after the difficulties of the 1970s.

The TGV's success encouraged the construction of further high-speed lines in France and in other countries. The Atlantic line, opened in 1989, connected Paris with the west of France, and the Nord line, opened in 1993, linked Paris with Lille and the Channel Tunnel. The TGV network expanded across France and into neighbouring countries, and it became one of the most important means of travel between major cities. The TGV's operating model, with its combination of dedicated high-speed lines and conventional lines for freight and regional traffic, became a common pattern in European railway planning. The TGV also set records for speed, reaching 515.3 kilometres per hour in a test run in 1990 and 574.8 kilometres per hour in 2007, which remains the record for a wheel-on-rail train.

The Channel Tunnel, which opened in 1994, linked Britain and France by a rail tunnel beneath the English Channel. The tunnel was a major engineering achievement, and it made possible the Eurostar service between London, Paris, and Brussels. The Eurostar was operated by a consortium of railway companies, and it was among the first international high-speed services in Europe. The tunnel and the Eurostar changed travel between Britain and the continent, reducing the journey between London and Paris to a few hours and offering an alternative to air travel for many passengers. The project was financially difficult, and it took many years to recover its costs, but it demonstrated the potential of international high-speed rail.

The European Union, through its transport policy, promoted the development of a trans-European high-speed network, and it funded several major projects. The German ICE, introduced in 1991, was the German equivalent of the TGV, and it was built to run on a combination of new and upgraded lines. Italy's Direttissima line, opened in the 1970s and upgraded later, and Spain's AVE network, begun in the 1990s and linking Madrid with Seville and Barcelona, also became important parts of the European system. Spain built one of the largest high-speed networks in the world in a relatively short time, and the AVE became a symbol of the country's modernisation. The European high-speed network is now extensive, although it is not uniform, and some countries have built more lines than others.

The integration of high-speed rail with the wider transport system has been an important theme in European policy. Interoperability, in which trains from one country can run on the networks of another, has required common standards for signalling, power supply, and safety. The European Rail Traffic Management System, known as ERTMS, is an effort to create a unified signalling standard across the continent, and it is gradually being installed on high-speed and main lines. The challenge of creating a seamless European network has been large, and it reflects the enduring fragmentation of railway systems across national borders.

## High-Speed Rail in Asia and Beyond

China's high-speed railway programme has been the largest in the world, and it has transformed the country's transport system in less than two decades. The first Chinese high-speed lines were built in the early 2000s, and the country began importing and adapting technology from Japan, Germany, France, and Canada. The Beijing to Tianjin line, opened in 2008 and designed for speeds of 350 kilometres per hour, was the first dedicated high-speed line in China, and it was followed by a rapid expansion of the network. By the early 2020s China had built more than forty thousand kilometres of high-speed railway, and the network connected most of the country's major cities. The Chinese programme has been notable for its scale, its speed of construction, and its use of domestic manufacturing to produce trains and infrastructure.

The Chinese high-speed network has changed patterns of travel and settlement in the country. Journeys that once took days by train now take hours, and cities that were once remote are now connected to the national economy. The network has also been criticised for its cost and for the debt that some of the operating companies have incurred. The debate over whether the investment has been economically justified is ongoing, but the scale of the network is undeniable, and it has shown how high-speed rail can be used as a tool of regional development and national integration.

South Korea opened its first high-speed line, the Gyeongbu line, in 2004, using a French-derived design that was later adapted to local conditions. Taiwan opened a high-speed line in 2007 with Japanese technology, and it has used the line to link major cities along the western corridor of the island. India has been planning high-speed lines for many years, and the Mumbai to Ahmedabad line, which has been under development with Japanese support, is intended to be among the first of its kind in the country. The spread of high-speed rail across Asia shows that the technology is no longer confined to a few wealthy countries, and that many nations regard it as a means of modernisation.

In the United States, high-speed rail has been discussed for decades, and the Northeast Corridor between Washington and Boston has seen the most significant efforts. The Acela Express, introduced in 2000, runs at speeds of up to about 150 miles per hour on sections of track, but the line's infrastructure does not allow sustained high-speed operation over its full length, and the service has been limited by the condition of the track and the need for shared use with freight and commuter trains. Proposals for dedicated high-speed networks in California and elsewhere have been debated, and some projects have been started, but the American experience has been slower than the Asian and European experience, reflecting differences in politics, finance, and geography.

Magnetic levitation, or maglev, offers an alternative to conventional wheel-on-rail high-speed trains. Maglev trains float above a guideway, supported and propelled by magnetic forces, and they avoid the friction of the wheel on the rail. The German Transrapid, developed in the 1970s and 1980s, was tested extensively, and a commercial line was opened in Shanghai in 2004 to connect the city with its airport. The Shanghai Maglev, which runs about thirty kilometres, reaches speeds of up to about 431 kilometres per hour in service, and it is one of the fastest commercial trains in the world. Japan has developed the superconducting SCMaglev system, which reached a speed of 603 kilometres per hour in a manned test in 2015, and it has been planned as a line between Tokyo and Nagoya and eventually Osaka. The maglev has not yet become a widespread form of transport, because of its cost and the need for dedicated guideways, but it remains a significant technological option for the future.

## Freight, Heavy Haul, and the Economics of the Modern Railway

While high-speed passenger trains have attracted the most public attention, freight remains the largest part of the railway business in most countries, and it has undergone profound changes over the past century. The development of standardised containers, which began in the 1950s and was championed by Malcolm McLean in the United States, revolutionised the handling of goods. Containers could be moved by ship, rail, and road without being unpacked, and they allowed a far more efficient integration of transport modes. Intermodal rail, in which containers are carried on trains between ports and inland terminals, became a central part of the logistics system, and it has been a major source of growth for railways in many countries.

Heavy-haul railways, which carry very large loads of bulk commodities such as iron ore, coal, and grain over long distances, have been developed in Australia, Brazil, South Africa, and North America. These railways use long trains, sometimes several kilometres in length, with multiple locomotives distributed along the train and sophisticated control systems that manage the forces within the train. The Australian iron ore railways of the Pilbara region are among the most advanced heavy-haul systems in the world, and they carry some of the longest and heaviest trains in operation. Heavy haul has shown that the railway remains an efficient means of moving bulk goods over long distances, and it has contributed to the economic development of resource-rich regions.

The economics of the railway have been transformed by deregulation and privatisation in many countries. The United States passed the Staggers Rail Act in 1980, which relaxed price regulation and allowed railways to compete more effectively with trucks and barges. The act is often credited with restoring the financial health of American freight railways, which had been in serious decline in the 1970s, and it led to a consolidation of the industry into a small number of large companies. The American freight network is now one of the most productive in the world, and it carries a large share of the country's freight.

Britain privatised its railways in the 1990s, separating infrastructure from train operation and franchising passenger services to private companies. The privatisation was controversial, and it has been criticised for fragmentation, high fares, and problems with the management of the network. The infrastructure was placed in the hands of a private company, Railtrack, which was later replaced by a public body, Network Rail. The British experience has been studied by many countries, and it illustrates the difficulties of reforming a complex and interdependent system. Japan took a different path in 1987, when the national railway was divided into several regional companies, which were privatised, and the freight business was separated and operated by a different company. The Japanese reform was generally considered a success, and the regional companies have become profitable, especially on the Shinkansen network.

The railway's freight business faces competition from road transport, from air freight for high-value goods, and from the shift toward services rather than goods in advanced economies. Railways have responded by improving their speed and reliability, by investing in intermodal terminals, and by developing new markets. The growing concern over climate change has also encouraged governments to promote rail as a low-carbon alternative to road and air transport, and many countries now include railway investment in their climate policies. The railway's energy efficiency per tonne-kilometre remains high, and this advantage has become more important in a world concerned with carbon emissions.

## The Railway and the Future

The railway has been a long and continuous presence in the economic and social life of many countries, and its future is likely to be shaped by several trends. The first is the growing demand for high-speed travel between cities, which has encouraged the construction of new lines and the upgrading of existing ones. The second is the increasing importance of decarbonisation, which has led to the electrification of more lines and the use of renewable energy to power trains. The third is the development of digital technology, which is transforming signalling, maintenance, and passenger information. Automatic train operation, in which trains run without drivers on some routes, is already in use on several urban metros, and it may spread to main lines in the future.

The railway also faces the challenge of financing. Building and maintaining a railway is expensive, and the costs of high-speed lines in particular are very large. The fiscal capacity of governments, the willingness of private investors to commit capital to long-term projects, and the political support needed to build infrastructure all affect the rate at which railways can expand. The experience of the past two centuries suggests that railways have been most successful when they have been supported by a clear public purpose and a stable framework of regulation and investment, but the design of such frameworks remains a difficult task.

The social dimension of the railway should not be forgotten. The railway has been a means of mobility for millions of people, and it has shaped the lives of those who worked on it as drivers, signalmen, track workers, and station staff. Railway workers have often been organised into trade unions, and the history of the railway is also a history of labour struggles over pay, hours, and safety. The railway has also been a symbol of national identity and public pride, and its stations, trains, and lines have often been the subject of art, literature, and photography. The history of the railway is therefore not only a history of engineering and economics but also of human experience.

The railway began as a way of moving coal and iron along a wooden track, and it has grown into a system that carries people at speeds of over three hundred kilometres per hour and moves goods across continents. Its development has been shaped by the availability of materials, the ingenuity of engineers, the needs of industry, the decisions of governments, and the choices of travellers. Each stage of its history has built on the previous one, and each has left a legacy in the form of infrastructure, machines, institutions, and habits of thought. The wagonway of the Tyne and the high-speed line of the Tōkaidō are separated by more than two centuries, but they are part of the same continuous story, in which the guided wheel and the steam engine have been transformed again and again into new forms.
